newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban pushed back further in Salang Pass.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban pushed back further in Salang Pass.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia appears to have suffered further reverses at the hands of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood in fighting in the Salang Pass north of Kabul, witnesses said on Thursday.
The witnesses said the sound of heavy fighting was apparent just north of Jabal-os-Siraj, a town at the foot of the Hindu Kush mountains through which the steep-sided pass leads.
"It was very close to Jabal-os-Siraj," said one traveller, who asked not to be identified.

On Wednesday, the front line was about 15 km (nine miles) north of Jabal-os-Siraj, witnesses said. Before Masood's men launched a surprise attack on Tuesday, the front line had been another 15 km to 20 km (nine to 12 miles) further north.
Confirmation of the reports was not immediately available.

Western reporters were barred from travelling to the area. Nervous Taleban fighters manning a roadblock just south of the town of Charikar, about 30 minutes drive from Jabal-os-Siraj, said they had orders to turn them back.
On Tuesday, Taleban battlefield commander in the Salang, Maulavi Khairulla Haqani, told Reuters Television that his men had stemmed the advance of Masood's ethnic Tajik fighters down the Salang.

He said fighting had been fierce, but declined to comment on casualties. Western aid workers, however, quoted witnesses as saying they had seen at least 100 Taleban bodies and many more wounded being taken to Jabal-os-Siraj.

The attack forced the Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, to break off their attempt to enter Masood's Panjsher valley fortress. The Taleban have swiftly taken control of about three-quarters of Afghanistan since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago,

Their assault on Panjsher started on Saturday, but by Wednesday evening not a single black-turbanned Taleban fighter was to be seen in the town of Golbahar. The town sits about 10 km (six miles) east of Jabal-os-Siraj and astride the rocky gorge leading into the valley.
Days of heavy fighting had taken Taleban fighters only about 500 metres (yards) into the gorge, which Masood had blocked with landslides.

In the Salang, there was no word on casualties among Masood's men. They were led by his former area commander, Basir Solangi, in an attack down the pass and over the mountainsides that cut off a large number of Taleban fighters, the aid workers said.
When the Taleban, most of them ethnic Pushtun, drove north after taking Kabul, Solangi retreated north into territory controlled by Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Dostum, who controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, has held talks with ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani this week and said Masood was expected to join them.
Karim Khallili, leader of the Hezb-i-Wahadat faction that controls territory west of Jabal-os-Siraj, was also in Mazar-i-Sharif.
The Taleban leadership in Kabul dismissed any possibility of an alliance between the groups, which have been enemies in the past.

But Solangi's attack in the Salang, where he destroyed a Soviet battalion in the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist government in Kabul, suggested cooperation already existed on the ground because the assault could not have been launched without Dostum's approval, Afghan watchers said.
"It could be a message to the Taleban, with Dostum demonstrating what is possible without his men getting involved directly and putting pressure on the Taleban to negotiate on his terms," said one.
"However, it seems more likely at this stage the possibility of an alliance is real and the Taleban would be in serious trouble if it happened."
Jabal-os-Siraj would be vulnerable. Masood, who managed to withdraw from Kabul with most of his armour, could hit it from the east.

Dostum, with an army of several thousand experienced men and a small air force, could join in from the north. The Hezb-i-Wahadat, a Moslem Shia group opposed to the Sunni Taleban, could attack from the west.
South of Jabal-os-Siraj, a flat plateau runs south before dropping into the Kabul valley. The Taleban appear to have no defensive lines between the two.

However, the witnesses said the Taleban appeared to be strengthening a base just south of Jabal-os-Siraj, moving in a Russian-built Ouragan mobile rocket launcher with a 40 km (25 mile) range along with several artillery pieces. All are pointed at the Salang, the witnesses said.
